documents.unit: AI Resource Hub / AI Working Group
documents.title: Santa Clara University AI Guidelines
documents.summary: University-wide guidelines for the whole SCU community on AI use. They require data protection, verification of outputs, bias checks and TAR approval of tools, and state that the university has no university-wide course AI policy, so faculty set it; a research section and a note on AI detectors are included.
documents.stance_why: The guidelines state that 'the University does not have a university-wide policy for AI use across courses and curricula' and that 'Faculty are expected to clearly communicate their policies and rationales', so the coursework decision is handed to faculty, while general rules (data, accuracy, bias) bind everyone; stance is delegates.

units.why: The page opens by calling itself a 'work in progress' as 'the technology, the law and the University community usage evolves', so it commits to revision; this is a governance statement (P54) that informs rather than directs.
units.anchor: these guidelines are a

units.why: 'committed to actively and ethically engaging with artificial intelligence' states the university-wide purpose and principle of the guidelines, so it is an institution-level framework (P56), not a rule on use.
units.anchor: committed to actively and ethically engaging with artificial intelligence

units.why: The sentence that AI must be used 'consistent with University policies and applicable laws, protects our confidential information' sets a general compliance expectation, so P77 (comply with law and policy) fits; the confidentiality part is coded separately below.
units.anchor: use AI in a manner that is consistent with University policies and applicable laws

units.why: 'While the University supports the responsible use of AI' is the university's general position toward AI use: supported if responsible. It is a principle in the framework, not a tiered rule.
units.anchor: While the University supports the responsible use of AI

units.why: The risk bullet 'if an AI tool is given access to personal information, the technology may not respect the privacy rights' explains a privacy hazard; it informs and belongs with data protection (P50).
units.anchor: if an AI tool is given access to personal information, the technology may not respect

units.why: 'the University may lose its intellectual property (“IP”) rights' describes the risk of entering confidential information into AI; it is a rationale for protecting confidential data, so P50.
units.anchor: the University may lose its intellectual property
units.fit_note: The risk is loss of IP rights and disclosure to third parties of confidential information and trade secrets, which P50 does not name separately.

units.why: 'AI outputs may violate the IP rights of others, and might not themselves be protected by IP laws' is a statement about copyright and ownership of AI output, which is what P52 covers.
units.anchor: AI outputs may violate the IP rights of others

units.why: 'AI outputs might be factually inaccurate' with liability if relied on without review is the accuracy risk; P31 covers 'AI output can be wrong'.
units.anchor: AI outputs might be factually inaccurate

units.why: 'AI may produce decisions that are biased, discriminatory' names a bias harm, which is P53.
units.anchor: AI may produce decisions that are biased, discriminatory

units.why: The scope paragraph says the Guidelines cover 'faculty, researchers, postdoctoral scholars, staff, students, volunteers, and trainees', defining who is bound; it is the scope part of an institution-wide framework (P56).
units.anchor: provide guidance on the use of AI tools by faculty, researchers, postdoctoral scholars, staff, students

units.why: 'SCU community members are encouraged to regularly review the most recent version' tells readers the guidelines will be updated and to re-check them, so P54 (revisit regularly).
units.anchor: encouraged to regularly review the most recent version of these Guidelines

units.why: 'obtain TAR approval before purchasing (or acquiring for free) AI products' is a mandatory review step with 'vendor risk, legal and accessibility review', which is institutional review of AI vendors (P65).
units.anchor: obtain TAR approval before purchasing (or acquiring for free) AI products
units.fit_note: It covers acquiring any AI tool, even free ones, through the Technology Acquisition Request process; P65 is about vendor agreements and data sharing.

units.why: 'must not enter Level One Data or Level Two Data ... into any public or unapproved AI tool' is a prohibition on entering confidential and personal data, which is P50's data-protection rule.
units.anchor: must not enter Level One Data or Level Two Data
units.policy: SCU community members must not enter Level One Data or Level Two Data (including personal and confidential information) into any public or unapproved AI tool.

units.why: The text says approved data classes 'may be used in an AI tool only if the tool has been approved ... through the TAR process', which pairs data protection with using vetted tools (P50).
units.anchor: Such data may be used in an AI tool only if the tool has been

units.why: 'SCU community members may enter Level Three Data into public AI tools' permits public data in public tools; it is the flip side of the privacy rule and fits P50 only partly because it grants permission.
units.anchor: may enter Level Three Data into public AI tools
units.policy: SCU community members may enter Level Three Data into public AI tools.
units.fit_note: It permits entry of Level Three data into public tools, and says anything given to public tools should be treated as public.

units.why: 'must verify and validate each element of output from AI tools to ensure there is a human audit' orders verification of AI output because it 'may be inaccurate, incomplete, or fabricated', which is P31.
units.anchor: must verify and validate each element of output from AI tools

units.why: 'are responsible for any content published that includes AI-generated material' places responsibility for what is published on the user, which is P29 (own what you submit).
units.anchor: are responsible for any content published that includes AI-generated material
units.fit_note: It is about published content in general, not only student submissions.

units.why: 'regularly stress test their AI tools' asks users to probe tools with simple and expert queries to learn their limitations; nearest is P31 (AI output can be wrong) but it is about learning the tool's weaknesses.
units.anchor: users should regularly stress test their AI tools
units.fit_note: It recommends actively testing tools with simple and expert queries to learn error types, rather than only verifying outputs.

units.why: 'must consider whether the data input into, and the output of, AI tools produces decisions that may result in a disparate impact' requires a bias check on protected classes, and 'Do not rely on any output that is indicative of a potential bias' forbids reliance; both are P53 bias concerns.
units.anchor: must consider whether the data input into, and the output of, AI tools produces decisions

units.why: 'Do not represent AI-generated content as solely your own work where credit or sourcing is required (e.g., academic submissions...' bans passing off AI content as one's own. It is about crediting AI, so I chose P24 (disclose/cite); P19 would fit only if it banned generating the work.
units.anchor: Do not represent AI-generated content as solely your own work
units.fit_note: Framed as a ban on representing AI content as solely one's own where credit is required, including academic submissions and source coding.

units.why: 'SCU community members are expected to exercise it and opt out of training' tells users to use available opt-outs, a data-protection step (P50).
units.anchor: expected to exercise it and opt out of training

units.why: 'encouraged to use structured prompting frameworks with more tailored prompting' recommends skilled prompting for better outputs; P44 (effective AI use as a skill) is nearest.
units.anchor: encouraged to use structured prompting frameworks with more tailored prompting
units.fit_note: It is advice on prompt quality (roles, audience, context), not about employer expectations.

units.why: The Information Services team 'intends to publish a list of specific applications that have been vetted by the University' announces a vetted-tool list, matching P50's 'prefer university-vetted tools'.
units.anchor: intends to publish a list of specific applications that have been vetted by the University

units.why: 'should only enable Zoom AI Companion and other TAR approved tools with contractual protections' limits meeting assistants to vetted tools, i.e. P50.
units.anchor: should only enable Zoom AI Companion and other TAR approved tools

units.why: 'all meeting participants are aware of and consent to the meeting being recorded / transcribed' sets a consent rule for AI note-takers. It is a privacy rule, so P50, though it is about participants' consent rather than data classes.
units.anchor: all meeting participants are aware of and consent
units.fit_note: Consent of all participants before recording or transcribing is required, which P50 does not state.

units.why: 'If confidential data will be discussed, AI meeting assistants must not be used' bans a tool in a defined situation to protect confidential data (P50).
units.anchor: AI meeting assistants must not be used

units.why: The coursework section says deep learning 'could be undermined with the utilization of AI-generated content being passed off as one's own work'; this is a rationale that AI shortcuts learning, so P41, with a fit note since it also invokes integrity.
units.anchor: it is our shared responsibility to promote intellectual honesty and scholarly integrity
units.fit_note: Also frames the concern as intellectual honesty and passing off AI content as one's own.

units.why: The quoted Provost text says 'the University does not have a university-wide policy for AI use across courses and curricula', so the decision is left to faculty: P04 and a delegating stance.
units.anchor: the University does not have a university-wide policy for AI use across courses and curricula

units.why: 'Faculty have a responsibility to weigh the humanistic, ethical, and pedagogical considerations when determining how and whether to integrate AI' puts the decision with faculty; P04.
units.anchor: The faculty have a responsibility to weigh the humanistic, ethical, and pedagogical considerations

units.why: 'ensure that AI is facilitating and not replacing learning' states the criterion faculty must apply; it is the principle that AI must not replace learning, nearest P32.
units.anchor: ensure that AI is facilitating and not replacing learning
units.fit_note: The criterion is applied by faculty when deciding how to integrate AI, alongside accessibility and doing 'more good than harm'.

units.why: 'Faculty are expected to clearly communicate their policies and rationales for AI use in their courses and assignments' requires a stated policy and its reasons, which is P09.
units.anchor: Faculty are expected to clearly communicate their policies and rationales for AI use
units.fit_note: Also asks for the rationale, not only the rule.

units.why: 'expect students to maintain academic integrity and live up to student codes of conduct' binds students to existing integrity rules, i.e. P77.
units.anchor: expect students to maintain academic integrity and live up to student codes of conduct

units.why: 'There are risks of misidentification, which can have consequences in the classroom' warns about AI-detection tools; 'especially given the number of false positives' says they are unreliable. This fits P39.
units.anchor: there are risks of misidentification, which can have consequences in the classroom

units.why: 'AI detection should be treated as a guideline and not a grading metric' limits how detector output may be used; it is not a ban, so P39 (do not rely on detectors) fits.
units.anchor: AI detection should be treated as a guideline and not a grading metric

units.why: 'include the use of these tools in any discussion with students around course policies' asks instructors to tell students about detectors used; the nearest is P47 (disclose instructor AI use), though it concerns detection tools.
units.anchor: include the use of these tools in any discussion with students around course policies
units.fit_note: Applies to detection tools: say why and how they may be used in the course ('Proactive transparency').

units.why: 'Establishing clear escalation language, processes, and guidelines in the event of detected plagiarism, at the department level is important' asks departments to define escalation; it concerns the integrity process, P36.
units.anchor: Establishing clear escalation language, processes, and guidelines in the event of detected plagiarism
units.fit_note: It asks departments to write escalation processes, rather than classifying AI use as misconduct.

units.why: 'in an open and educational manner' for conversations with students about suspected misuse is an educative, not punitive, response (P68).
units.anchor: initiate and engage in such conversations with students in an open and educational manner

units.why: 'individuals who use AI in research should be transparent regarding its use, in describing methods, acknowledgements' is a research-disclosure rule; P62 (research) rather than P24 since it governs scholarship.
units.anchor: should be transparent regarding its use, in describing methods, acknowledgements

units.why: 'Researchers are responsible for the accuracy of any content created by AI that is included in any research output' sets researcher accountability for AI content, inside the research domain (P62).
units.anchor: Researchers are responsible for the accuracy of any content created by AI
units.fit_note: Includes the warning that AI invents citations and images and that AI citation checkers are inaccurate.

units.why: 'Researchers are expected to follow the policies of journals, funding agencies and professional societies' defers to venue and funder rules, as P62 states.
units.anchor: Researchers are expected to follow the policies of journals, funding agencies and professional societies

units.why: 'Researchers must avoid uploading ... any unpublished research data or other confidential information into an unauthorized AI tool' is a research-data rule, P62, with privacy angle.
units.anchor: must avoid uploading, or using as input, any unpublished research data

units.why: 'The National Institutes of Health (NIH) and U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), among others, prohibit using AI tools for peer review' reports that funders ban AI in peer review, a research rule (P62).
units.anchor: prohibit using AI tools for peer review

units.why: 'inputting interview data into an unauthorized AI tool ... creates the possibility that ... subjects could also be identified' warns about research-subject privacy; P62 research domain.
units.anchor: the personal information of research subjects
units.fit_note: Specific to the personal information of research subjects.

units.why: 'Researchers should be mindful that the output of AI tools may infringe the rights of third parties' is a research-context copyright caution, P52.
units.anchor: Researchers should be mindful that the output of AI tools may infringe the rights of

units.why: 'Researchers should comply with the expectations of their respective school, department and sub-discipline' defers to local rules and lists documentation duties; P62.
units.anchor: should comply with the expectations of their respective school, department and sub-discipline

units.why: 'Citing AI tools used and clearly explaining their specific contributions rather than presenting AI-generated content as your own work' is a citation duty in research; P62 for the domain, with P24 being the generic disclosure type.
units.anchor: Citing AI tools used and clearly explaining their specific contributions

units.why: 'creating an audit trail by tracking the AI tools used, prompts, exact steps taken to independently verify every claim' asks researchers to keep records of tools, prompts and verification, close to P26 but in research (P62).
units.anchor: creating an audit trail by tracking the AI tools used, prompts
units.fit_note: Documents verification of AI-generated citations, an audit trail of tools and prompts.

units.why: 'All University research is subject to the University's research integrity policies, such as the Policy on Research Misconduct' places AI-in-research under existing policy, P77.
units.anchor: All University research is subject to the University

units.why: 'should always keep in mind the usual rules and policies concerning privacy, honor code, academic integrity, research conduct' tells people AI use stays under existing policies, which is P77.
units.anchor: should always keep in mind the usual rules and policies concerning privacy, honor code, academic

units.why: 'Students should review the policies relating to academic integrity in the Student Conduct Code' points students to the code for AI integrity rules, P77.
units.anchor: Students should review the policies relating to academic integrity in the

units.why: 'the University's specific schools may also have additional rules and policies' says school rules layer over the university guidelines. No type covers layering of rules by unit.
units.anchor: the University's specific schools may also have additional rules and policies
units.uncovered_note: School-level rules may add to the university guidelines (layering of policy levels).

documents.title: AI Syllabus Policy
documents.summary: A library guide that helps faculty write syllabus AI statements, offering a permitted branch with sample situations and parameters and a not-permitted branch with sample reasons. It says SCU has no campus-wide AI policy and that the page only suggests wording.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'Santa Clara University currently does not have a campus wide AI policy' and that the library 'does not participate in syllabus creation or standards', and it offers permitted and not-permitted statements for faculty to pick, so it sets no stance itself: delegates.

units.why: 'Santa Clara University currently does not have a campus wide AI policy' states no university-wide rule exists, so the decision rests with faculty ('encouraged to determine how AI tools ... are utilized'); P04.
units.anchor: Santa Clara University currently does not have a campus wide AI policy

units.why: 'Faculty are encouraged to determine how AI tools and systems are utilized in their classrooms and communicate this to their students' gives each instructor the decision and asks them to communicate it. P04, with communication also in P09.
units.anchor: Faculty are encouraged to determine how AI tools and systems are utilized in their classrooms

units.why: 'by not having an AI statement in your syllabus you create ambiguous expectations' recommends an AI statement in every syllabus, P09.
units.anchor: by not having an AI statement in your syllabus you create ambiguous expectations

units.why: 'your goal is to be as clear and direct as possible to avoid ambiguity' asks for clear wording of the statement; P09 (state expectations) rather than P66 as no discussion is asked.
units.anchor: your goal is to be as clear and direct as possible to avoid ambiguity

units.why: The sample 'Graded assignments with specified Generative AI tools are allowed, as described in the syllabus' is one scenario in a menu of statements, where AI is allowed on named assignments; P04 (per assignment).
units.anchor: Graded assignments with specified Generative AI tools are allowed, as described in the syllabus

units.why: 'we will go over in class how to access and use them' says the instructor teaches students to use the allowed tools, so P44 (courses teach AI use).
units.anchor: we will go over in class how to access and use them

units.why: 'because students need to understand issues around privacy, data security, and consent' gives the reason for allowing specified tools; it is a privacy rationale, P50.
units.anchor: students need to understand issues around privacy, data security, and consent when using Generative AI
units.fit_note: Used as the stated reason for allowing specified tools: students need to learn about privacy, security and consent.

units.why: 'Ungraded assignments are allowed because students can augment their learning outside of class but still need to demonstrate mastery of skills without the support of Generative AI on graded assignments' sorts AI by graded or ungraded; P05 tiers by assessment type.
units.anchor: Ungraded assignments are allowed because students can augment their learning outside of class
units.fit_note: Also says graded work must be done without AI.

units.why: 'Self-study outside of the classroom is allowed because Generative AI can enhance learning' permits AI for self-study, P12/P14. P14 (study aids) chosen since it is self-directed study.
units.anchor: Self-study outside of the classroom is allowed because Generative AI can enhance learning

units.why: 'Use of AI is only allowed under special circumstances in which individual students approach the instructor on a case-by-case basis' is a permission-by-request scenario, P10 (ask first).
units.anchor: individual students approach the instructor on a case-by-case basis to develop a learning approach
units.fit_note: Students approach the instructor to build an individual learning approach; AI is otherwise not allowed.

units.why: 'it is not allowed to be used during open book/note tests or quizzes' bans AI in assessments even if allowed elsewhere, P22.
units.anchor: it is not allowed to be used during open book/note tests or quizzes

units.why: 'if you are found to be using unpermitted resources during these exercises you will be violating the university's Student Code of Conduct' classes such use as a code violation, P36.
units.anchor: you will be violating the university's Student Code of Conduct

units.why: 'It is never acceptable to completely copy the work of generative AI' bans submitting AI output as is, P19.
units.anchor: It is never acceptable to completely copy the work of generative AI

units.why: 'It should only be used as a resource and not for plagiarism' limits AI to a resource, i.e. students stay the primary problem-solver, P32.
units.anchor: It should only be used as a resource and not for plagiarism

units.why: 'Take responsibility for the content' says students answer for inaccurate, offensive or biased AI content they submit: P29.
units.anchor: What you submit is your responsibility across these dimensions
units.fit_note: Responsibility extends to inaccuracy, offensive language and biased or unethical representations.

units.why: 'Do not enter private, sensitive, or copyrighted data from others into AI tools without their consent' is a privacy and copyright rule, P50.
units.anchor: Do not enter private, sensitive, or copyrighted data from others into AI tools without their

units.why: 'Provide clear attribution of your sources' requires attribution of AI use as set by the course, P24.
units.anchor: Provide clear attribution of your sources

units.why: 'utilize Generative AI without attribution ... can be seen as potential academic dishonesty and treated' under the Student Code of Conduct: failing to attribute is the violation, P28.
units.anchor: Any assignments that utilize Generative AI without attribution per the guidelines shared in this course
units.fit_note: Handled under the Student Code of Conduct (undergraduate) or school honor codes (graduate and professional).

units.why: 'communicate your reasoning to your students' tells instructors who ban AI to give reasons, P66.
units.anchor: communicate your reasoning to your students

units.why: 'assignments in this course have been designed to ensure that you personally develop and demonstrate the knowledge and skills ... without the use of Generative AI' is a sample reason for a ban: doing the work builds skill, P41.
units.anchor: personally develop and demonstrate the knowledge and skills associated with the learning outcomes

units.why: 'its use is viewed as counter to the specific learning objectives of this course' is a sample reason for a ban, also P41.
units.anchor: its use is viewed as counter to the specific learning objectives of this course

units.why: 'Content in this course is private, sensitive, or copyrighted and should never be entered into a Generative AI tool' bans uploading course content, P49.
units.anchor: should never be entered into a Generative AI tool

units.why: 'encourage students to speak with you directly to ensure their self-study does not interfere' tells instructors to invite students to ask about self-study: P10.
units.anchor: encourage students to speak with you directly to ensure their self-study does not interfere
units.fit_note: Directed at instructors who ban AI but see students using it for self-study.

units.why: The page links to a repository of syllabus policies and says it exists 'to assist faculty with navigating AI'; faculty support resources, P63.
units.anchor: this page aims to assist faculty with navigating AI for faculty

units.why: 'Addressing AI in Syllabus Statements is a great resource ... additional thought prompts to help you understand how to cultivate your course's policy' points instructors to guidance before setting a policy, P63.
units.anchor: additional thought prompts to help you understand how to cultivate your course

documents.title: AI Squared in Student Learning
tiers: Allowed for specific assignments, projects, or tasks
documents.summary: School of Engineering resource page for instructors, with advice on setting course AI policies, notes on detectors, assignment-redesign ideas, risks, four named sample statement types and department course examples (including COEN 11, COEN 346, ELEN/COEN 21, ELEN 520, MECH 121, MECH 294). Reporting goes through the existing integrity process.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'a "one-size-fits-all" approach to syllabus statements is not suitable' and gives four scenarios from 'Prohibited in all circumstances' to 'Allowed with attribution' for instructors to adapt, so the school sets no single stance: delegates with tiers.

units.why: 'think about whether the use of generative AI tools in your course would support the learning goals of your course' tells instructors to decide by learning goals, P04.
units.anchor: think about whether the use of generative AI tools in your course would support the

units.why: 'It is important to examine the learning outcomes of your courses and adopt a suitable AI policy' asks for an AI policy for each course, P09.
units.anchor: examine the learning outcomes of your courses and adopt a suitable AI policy
units.fit_note: The policy is to be derived from the course learning outcomes.

units.why: 'none that are highly recommended in industry with a high accuracy rate' says detectors are inaccurate, P39.
units.anchor: there are none that are highly recommended in industry with a high accuracy rate

units.why: 'Many of them struggle with high rate detection on a material that is human written' notes false positives, P39.
units.anchor: Many of them struggle with high rate detection on a material that is human written

units.why: The list 'Ways to circumvent many of the detector tools' (reword phrases, replace variable names) shows detectors are easily defeated, P39.
units.anchor: Ways to circumvent many of the detector tools

units.why: 'There currently isn't any tool that I found that is geared towards detecting written code' states there is no reliable code detector, P39.
units.anchor: any tool that I found that is geared towards detecting written code

units.why: 'It might take using two or more tools in conjunction to further increase result accuracy' suggests combining detectors, i.e. use of detection tools (P40), with some caution about trust.
units.anchor: It might take using two or more tools in conjunction to further increase result accuracy
units.fit_note: The page also doubts the tools' accuracy, so it does not endorse relying on them.

units.why: The page lists 'Popular AI Detectors' and then those 'that have reputation for having the most accurate results' (GPTZero, Originality.ai); this is a named list of detection tools for instructors, P40.
units.anchor: AI detectors that have reputation for having the most accurate results

units.why: 'Having students complete assignments and exams during class (in person)' lists in-class assessment as a response to AI, P33.
units.anchor: Having students complete assignments and exams during class (in person)

units.why: 'Asking more nuanced questions that may be beyond the capabilities of the current AI tools' is an assignment redesign idea, P35.
units.anchor: Asking more nuanced questions that may be beyond the capabilities of the current AI tools

units.why: 'Requiring students to show intermediate results of their assignments or projects before they submit their finished work' is a process-based redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Requiring students to show intermediate results of their assignments or projects

units.why: 'Supplementing written assignments with additional oral presentations' checks understanding through explanation, P34.
units.anchor: Supplementing written assignments with additional oral presentations, flowcharts, concept maps, group work, case studies
units.fit_note: Also lists flowcharts, concept maps, group work and case studies as alternative formats.

units.why: 'You may not enter internal, sensitive or restricted data into any generative AI tool or service' bans entering restricted data, P50.
units.anchor: You may not enter internal, sensitive or restricted data into any generative AI tool or

units.why: 'It is advisable for users to independently verify information obtained from generative AI' is advice to verify output, P31.
units.anchor: It is advisable for users to independently verify information obtained from generative AI

units.why: 'Generative AI may inadvertently mirror biases present in its training data' and users should 'critically assess' responses; bias, P53.
units.anchor: Generative AI may inadvertently mirror biases present in its training data

units.why: 'there remains a possibility that generative AI may produce or respond to content that is offensive, inappropriate' names inappropriate-content harm, P53.
units.anchor: generative AI may produce or respond to content that is offensive, inappropriate

units.why: 'Automated Scoring: ChatGPT can be effectively used to assess student papers and essays' suggests AI for assessing student work, an instructor use. P59 not P46 because it does not say who decides the grade.
units.anchor: ChatGPT can be effectively used to assess student papers and essays
units.fit_note: Offered as an example from medical education; grade decision responsibility is not addressed.

units.why: 'ChatGPT is its ability to generate exercises, quizzes and scenarios that can be used in the classroom' suggests AI to make teaching materials, P59.
units.anchor: ability to generate exercises, quizzes and scenarios that can be used in the classroom

units.why: 'ChatGPT can be used to create virtual tutors or assistants that can answer students' questions' suggests AI tutor bots, P17.
units.anchor: ChatGPT can be used to create virtual tutors or assistants
units.fit_note: An example of what AI could do in medical education, not an adopted SCU tool.

units.why: 'ChatGPT can also be utilized to assist students in their research by answering questions and providing summaries of texts' lists AI as a research and study aid, P14.
units.anchor: assist students in their research by answering questions and providing summaries of texts

units.why: 'create content for summaries, quizzes, and flashcards' lists AI-made study content, P14.
units.anchor: create content for summaries, quizzes, and flashcards

units.why: 'ChatGPT can help with the capstone projects for Suggesting experimental techniques' suggests AI for exploring approaches in capstone work, P15.
units.anchor: ChatGPT can help with the capstone projects for
units.policy: ChatGPT can help with capstone projects by suggesting experimental techniques, suggesting mathematical models, writing the introduction and analyzing results.
units.fit_note: Also lists writing an introduction and analyzing results.

units.why: 'Assign a role to ChatGPT' with the other prompting steps (be clear, give context, ask follow-ups) is advice on effective prompting, P44.
units.anchor: Assign a role to ChatGPT
units.policy: A step-by-step approach for communicating with ChatGPT: assign it a role, be clear and concise, provide context, use specific keywords and ask follow-up questions.
units.fit_note: Prompting steps, not employer expectations.

units.why: 'a "one-size-fits-all" approach to syllabus statements is not suitable' places the decision at course level, P04.
units.anchor: approach to syllabus statements is not suitable since each discipline and course has its own

units.why: 'SCU's Academic Integrity policy underscores the importance of each instructor's responsibility to clearly communicate our own policies in the syllabus' makes the syllabus the place for the policy, P09.
units.anchor: responsibility to clearly communicate our own policies in the syllabus
units.policy: SCU's Academic Integrity policy underscores the importance of each instructor's responsibility to clearly communicate our own policies in the syllabus.

units.why: 'Under what circumstances are generative AI tools allowed?' is one of the questions every statement should answer, P09.
units.anchor: Under what circumstances are generative AI tools allowed?
units.policy: Every syllabus statement should say under what circumstances generative AI tools are allowed.

units.why: 'What is the rationale or justification behind this policy?' asks the statement to include its reasons, P66.
units.anchor: What is the rationale or justification behind this policy?
units.policy: Every syllabus statement should give the rationale or justification behind the policy.

units.why: 'What are the consequences for students violating the course policy?' asks for penalties to be stated in the syllabus, P37.
units.anchor: What are the consequences for students violating the course policy?
units.policy: Every syllabus statement should state the consequences for students violating the course policy.
units.fit_note: It asks that consequences be stated, without naming any.

units.why: 'What are other forms of assistance and collaborative efforts acceptable?' asks the instructor to name allowed help and the assignments it applies to, P09.
units.anchor: What are other forms of assistance and collaborative efforts acceptable?
units.policy: Every syllabus statement should say what other forms of assistance and collaboration are acceptable and for which assignments.

units.why: 'Where and how should students disclose their use of AI?' asks instructors to set disclosure rules, P24.
units.anchor: Where and how should students disclose their use of AI?
units.policy: Every syllabus statement should say where and how students should disclose their use of AI.

units.why: 'You are encouraged to either adopt the provided examples or adapt it to fit your particular needs' invites instructors to reuse sample statements, P63.
units.anchor: You are encouraged to either adopt the provided examples or adapt it
